opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what we actually mean by intelligence. For a long time in AI, we built systems that were very good at one thing. You train a model on Go, it plays Go. You train it on Atari, it plays that game. But if you change the environment even slightly, it falls apart. That's not really generalization; that's memorizing a distribution very well.

What changed with language models, and especially with reasoning, is that the model can take something it learned in one setting, like how to break a problem into steps, how to check its own work, or how to backtrack when something isn't working, and apply it somewhere completely different. Maybe it learned to reason through math problems, and then you put it in a coding environment, or a web browsing task, or something it has never seen, and that thinking process still helps. To me that's the key signal. The skill isn't tied to the surface of the task. It's tied to something more abstract.

Humans work this way. You don't learn a separate way of thinking for every job. You learn to think, and then you bring that to whatever you're facing. When a model shows that same kind of transfer, it suggests it has learned something more fundamental than pattern matching on a specific benchmark.

There's also a practical reason I care about this. The real world isn't a fixed set of environments. If we want agents that are actually useful, doing real work for real people, we can't build a custom environment and reward for every possible task. There are too many. So the only scalable path is models that generalize, where reasoning learned in some places carries over to places we never trained on. Transfer between environments is basically the test of whether we're on that path or just building a longer list of narrow skills.

So when I see reasoning transfer, I don't think of it as a nice side effect. I think it's the main thing. It's the evidence that the prior from language and the ability to think actually combine into something general.

r002.rationale: It says generalization matters because real-world tasks are too numerous for custom environments and rewards; it does not say overfitting and generalization lose practical significance if a model can do everything.

r003.rationale: It describes learned reasoning skills transferring from one setting to different or unseen environments as evidence of genuine generalization.

r004.rationale: It mentions language models and a prior from language, but does not identify language as a universal medium for reasoning across environments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key insight is that reasoning itself is a kind of action, and it's a very special one, because it's the only action that is not bound to any particular environment.

When I was doing ReAct, the thing that really struck me was that a language model trained on internet text could go into a text game, or a web shopping task, or a question-answering setup with a Wikipedia API, and it would just work. Not perfectly, but it would work, with a few examples. Nothing about those environments was in the training data in the form of trajectories. What transferred was the ability to say, in natural language, "okay, I'm trying to find this item, the search result didn't show it, so let me try a different query." That sentence is useful in almost any environment that has a search box, and most of what makes it useful is not specific to the environment at all.

So why do I call that genuine generalization and not just pattern matching? Because the classic RL way of thinking, from the Atari era, is that you train an agent in one environment and the policy is basically a lookup from pixels to joystick moves. Change the game and it collapses. The policy has no room to represent "I don't know what this is, let me try something and see what happens." The action space is too narrow to express that. Language gives you an action space that is open-ended, and reasoning is the part of that action space that's about the agent's own state rather than about the world. When the model reasons, it's effectively doing a kind of inference-time adaptation: it looks at the observation, builds a little model of what's going on, and decides. That procedure is the same whether you're in a kitchen simulator or a terminal.

The honest caveat is that it's not magic. If the environment requires knowledge the model doesn't have, reasoning won't conjure it. And there's a real question of how much of the transfer is coming from pretraining versus the reasoning scaffold. But I think the direction is clear. If you train a model to reason across many diverse environments, what it learns is not "how to solve environment A" but "how to approach a new environment," and that's what we've always meant by generalization. The environments are the training data, and the reasoning is the prior that lets you do few-shot adaptation to the next one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pretraining and reasoning scaffolds but does not suggest reinforcement learning merely activates skills already present in pretraining.

r002.rationale: It does not claim the distinction between overfitting and generalization loses practical significance when a model can do everything in the world.

r003.rationale: It identifies the transfer of reasoning and ways of approaching a new environment as the basis for genuine generalization.

r004.rationale: It describes language as an open-ended action space and reasoning as an action not bound to a particular environment.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is whether the model has learned something that survives a change in the environment. If it can solve a problem only when the wording, tools, and feedback look like its training examples, it’s hard to distinguish reasoning from familiarity.

But suppose it encounters a new environment, with different actions and different ways of observing the results. If it can still break down the task, test a hypothesis, notice a mistake, and revise its plan, then something more general has transferred. It’s reusing a way of solving problems, rather than just a particular solution.

Of course, transfer alone isn’t conclusive. Two environments can look different while having almost identical underlying tasks. So the important question is what actually changed, and how much adaptation the model needed. I regard transfer as evidence of genuine generalization when the model can handle new constraints and use feedback to figure out what to do, without being trained specifically for that setting.

r001.rationale: The response does not suggest that pre-training already contains the relevant skills or that reinforcement learning merely activates them.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss the distinction between overfitting and generalization becoming practically insignificant if a model can do everything in the world.

r003.rationale: It describes reusing a way of solving problems in a new environment and identifies that transfer as evidence of genuine generalization.

r004.rationale: It mentions changes in wording but does not identify language as a universal medium for reasoning beyond a particular environment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is whether the model has learned something that survives a change in the environment. If you train and test on very similar problems, better performance could come from recognizing familiar patterns. That’s useful, but it doesn’t necessarily mean the model can apply the underlying reasoning elsewhere.

When the environment changes—the observations look different, the available actions change, or feedback comes in a different form—the model has to figure out how its existing knowledge applies. Can it still break down a problem, test a hypothesis, and revise its plan when something fails? If those abilities transfer, that’s stronger evidence that it has learned a reusable way of solving problems.

Of course, we should be careful about what counts as a different environment. Two tasks can look different and still share almost the same structure. So I would call transfer evidence of generalization, rather than proof of some universal reasoning ability. The more varied the environments, and the less task-specific help the model needs, the stronger that evidence becomes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transfer and reusable problem-solving, but says nothing about pre-training or reinforcement learning activating existing skills.

r002.rationale: It does not address whether overfitting versus generalization matters if a model can do everything in the world.

r003.rationale: It says that abilities such as breaking down problems, testing hypotheses, and revising plans transferring across environments is evidence of learning a reusable way to solve problems.

r004.rationale: It does not identify language as a universal medium for reasoning beyond a particular environment.
